name: Ho Chi Minh
info: Ho Chi Minh (Hồ Chí Minh, 1890–1969) was a Vietnamese communist revolutionary who founded the Indochinese Communist Party, led the Việt Minh against Japan and France and ruled North Vietnam as its president from 1946 until his death.

facts.born: 19 May 1890 (the generally accepted date; he also gave 1891, 1892, 1894 and 1895) in the village of Hoàng Trù, Kim Liên commune, Nghệ An province, as Nguyễn Sinh Cung; son of Nguyễn Sinh Sắc, a Confucian scholar and teacher, later an imperial magistrate
facts.died: 2 September 1969, of heart failure, at his home in Hanoi, aged 79; embalmed and displayed in a mausoleum in Ba Đình Square, against his wish to be cremated
facts.role: Founding member of the French Communist Party (1920); Comintern agent; founder of the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League (1925) and the Indochinese Communist Party (1930); leader of the Việt Minh (from 1941); prime minister (1945–1955) and president (1946–1969) of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam; party chairman until his death
facts.known: the Việt Minh and the August Revolution; the Declaration of Independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam (1945); the First Indochina War and Điện Biên Phủ; the land reform of 1953–1956 and its executions; the Hồ Chí Minh trail; the Vietnam War; the name "Uncle Ho"; his poems, among them the Prison Diary

t: Born Nguyễn Sinh Cung in Annam, in French Indochina, Hồ Chí Minh left in 1911 as a ship's kitchen helper and spent three decades abroad, becoming a founding member of the French Communist Party, a Comintern agent and in 1930 founder of the Indochinese Communist Party.

Returning in 1941, he led the Việt Minh, proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in 1945 and fought the French until their defeat at Điện Biên Phủ in 1954, after which he ruled North Vietnam as a one-party state.

His government suppressed rival nationalists and carried out a land reform with executions whose number historians still dispute; he backed the insurgency in the South through the Vietnam War and died in 1969, six years before North Vietnam won it.
dyk: Hồ is known to have used between 50 and 200 pseudonyms. He began regularly using the name Hồ Chí Minh, "Bright spirit" or "Clear will", only after his release from a Chinese prison in 1943.
ev: Born Nguyễn Sinh Cung in Kim Liên commune, Nghệ An province, in Annam, French Indochina
Sails from Saigon as a kitchen helper on the French steamer Amiral de Latouche-Tréville
Votes for the Third International at the Congress of Tours and becomes a founding member of the French Communist Party
Chairs the meeting in Hong Kong that unites two Vietnamese communist parties and founds the Indochinese Communist Party
Returns to Vietnam to lead the Việt Minh independence movement against the Japanese occupation
After the August Revolution, reads the Declaration of Independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam
The Việt Minh defeat the French at Điện Biên Phủ; the Geneva Accords divide Vietnam at the 17th parallel
Dies of heart failure at his home in Hanoi, with the outcome of the Vietnam War still in question

sections.early:
The details of Hồ Chí Minh's early life are uncertain: he used between 50 and 200 pseudonyms, and at least four official biographies differ on names, dates and places. He was born Nguyễn Sinh Cung in 1890 in the village of Hoàng Trù in Kim Liên commune, Nghệ An province, then under French protection; 1890 is generally accepted, though at various times he gave four other years. His father, Nguyễn Sinh Sắc, was a Confucian scholar and teacher who later became an imperial magistrate and was demoted for abuse of power after a local figure died following a caning; he was both a patriot and a collaborator with the French colonial state. Following Confucian tradition, his father renamed him Nguyễn Tất Thành at the age of ten.

He mastered chữ Hán, the prerequisite for any serious study of Confucianism, and then received a French education at the Collège Quốc học in Huế, which Phạm Văn Đồng, Võ Nguyên Giáp and his later rival Ngô Đình Diệm also attended. A tradition that he took part in an anti-corvée demonstration of 1908 is contradicted by a French archival document showing that he was admitted to the school months after it. In 1911, using the alias Văn Ba, he signed on as a kitchen helper on the French steamer Amiral de Latouche-Tréville and sailed from Saigon to Marseille. Refused by the French Colonial School, he spent the years to 1917 working on ships; by his own accounts he lived for a time in the United States and in London, though the evidence for much of it is thin.
sections.rise:
From 1919 Nguyễn Tất Thành took up politics in Paris. He joined the Groupe des Patriotes Annamites, which petitioned the Versailles peace talks, Georges Clemenceau and Woodrow Wilson among others, for the civil rights of the Vietnamese and an end to French rule. It was ignored, but as the public face of the petition, which Phan Văn Trường had written, he became known as Nguyễn Ái Quốc ("Nguyễn the Patriot"). Many authors have called 1919 a lost "Wilsonian moment", but he was already committed to a socialist program. In December 1920 he voted for the Third International at the Congress of Tours and became a founding member of the French Communist Party.

In 1923 he went to Moscow, worked for the Comintern and studied at the Communist University of the Toilers of the East. Sent to Canton, he organised the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League and trained young Vietnamese revolutionaries. After Chiang Kai-shek's anti-communist coup of 1927 he left Canton, and by way of Moscow, Europe and Thailand reached Hong Kong, where early in 1930 he chaired the meeting that united two Vietnamese communist parties and founded the Indochinese Communist Party. Arrested in Hong Kong in 1931, he was defended by the solicitor Frank Loseby and eventually released. In Moscow he was removed from control of the party he had founded, whose new leaders criticised his nationalist tendencies, but he returned to favour in 1937. In 1940 he and his lieutenants Võ Nguyên Giáp and Phạm Văn Đồng founded the League for Vietnamese Independence, the Việt Minh, in Guilin.
sections.deeds:
Hồ returned to Vietnam in 1941 to lead the Việt Minh against the Japanese occupation. Jailed in China by Chiang Kai-shek's local authorities and released in 1943, he began regularly using the name Hồ Chí Minh. In April 1945 he offered intelligence to the American Office of Strategic Services, which sent a team to train his men. After the August Revolution and the abdication of Emperor Bảo Đại, he read the Declaration of Independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September 1945. No country recognised his government, and President Harry S. Truman never answered his petitions. In March 1946, with 200,000 Chinese troops in the north, he signed an agreement recognising Vietnam as an autonomous state in the French Union, but it soon broke down. After the French Navy's bombardment of Haiphong, which reportedly killed more than 6,000 civilians, he declared war on 19 December 1946, beginning the First Indochina War.

His forces withdrew to the countryside and fought a guerrilla war. In February 1950 he met Joseph Stalin and Mao Zedong in Moscow, and they agreed that China would back the Việt Minh. In 1954 more than 10,000 French soldiers surrendered at Điện Biên Phủ, and the Geneva Accords divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with elections for reunification to be held in July 1956. Hồ's government became that of North Vietnam, a Communist-led one-party state, which he served as prime minister until 1955 and as president until his death. He also wrote poetry, among it Poems from the Prison Diary.
sections.opponents:
In 1946, while Hồ was abroad, his subordinates imprisoned 2,500 non-communist nationalists and forced 6,000 others to flee; hundreds of political opponents were executed or exiled after a failed coup attempt that July, and the Việt Minh collaborated with French forces to massacre supporters of rival nationalist movements and the Trotskyists. According to Daniel Guérin, Hồ called the Trotskyist leader Tạ Thu Thâu "a great patriot" and then added: "All those who do not follow the line which I have laid down will be broken." Arthur Dommen estimates that the Việt Minh killed between 100,000 and 150,000 civilians during the war; Benjamin Valentino estimates that the French were responsible for 60,000–250,000 civilian deaths.

The land reform of 1953–1956 was accompanied by executions of "reactionary and evil landlords". Estimates at the time ran to 50,000 or more; declassified Vietnamese and Hungarian documents point to far fewer, though likely more than 13,500, while Gareth Porter estimated 800–2,500 and Balázs Szalontai found 1,337 executions by December 1955, before a harsher third stage. In 1956 Hồ apologised for the serious errors of the reform, and as many as 23,748 political prisoners were released by September 1957.

The anti-communist writer Hoàng Văn Chí argued that Hồ betrayed the nationalist leader Phan Bội Châu to the French in 1925 for money; William Duiker rejected the charge, and Sophie Quinn-Judge and Duncan McCargo think it likely propaganda. The government remains sensitive to accounts of Hồ's private life and sought cuts in the translation of Duiker's biography.
sections.last:
From 1959 Hồ urged the Politburo to aid the Việt Cộng in the South, and a "people's war" was approved. North Vietnam built supply routes through Laos and Cambodia that became known as the Hồ Chí Minh trail, and in December 1960 created the National Liberation Front of South Vietnam. Hồ informally chose Lê Duẩn as the next party leader and in September 1960 stepped down as General Secretary, keeping a secondary role as head of state but considerable influence. In 1963 he showed interest in a French plan for a neutral federation of the two Vietnams, which faded after Diệm was overthrown and killed that November.

When American combat troops arrived and the bombing of the North began in 1965, Hồ insisted that there could be no peace talks unless the United States unconditionally stopped bombing, which he saw as a violation of North Vietnam's sovereignty. He made a secret visit to Mao in April 1965, and in 1967 agreed to the plan that became the Tet Offensive, wanting to see Vietnam reunified within his lifetime. In early 1969 he suffered a heart attack, and he answered a letter from President Richard Nixon without concessions. He died of heart failure at his home in Hanoi on 2 September 1969, aged 79. About 250,000 people attended his funeral, and his body was embalmed and put on display, against his will, which asked that he be cremated and his ashes scattered across a united Vietnam. North Vietnam won the war in 1975.
sections.legacy:
When North Vietnamese forces entered Saigon on 30 April 1975 their tanks carried the words "You are still marching with us, Uncle Hồ", and South Vietnam's former capital was renamed Ho Chi Minh City in his honour. His image hangs in public buildings and schoolrooms. William Duiker suggests that the cult of personality around him drew on traditions of authority in Vietnamese society, and that under Hồ Vietnamese Marxism developed as a kind of "reformed Confucianism". In Vietnamese folk religion some identify him with the Jade Emperor, a cult the government tolerates with unease; a movement founded in 2001 reportedly had around 24,000 followers by 2014.

Writers long argued whether he was fundamentally a nationalist or a communist; recent scholarship has shown his longstanding commitment to communist ideology, and official Vietnamese historiography rejects portrayals of him as merely a nationalist. His thought inspired leaders and movements in Asia, Africa and Latin America during decolonization, and as a communist he was relatively well regarded in the West. Time magazine included him in 1998 among the 100 most important people of the twentieth century, and in 1987 UNESCO recommended that its members mark the centenary of his birth. Places in Moscow, Saint Petersburg and Kolkata bear his name, and according to Vietnam's foreign ministry as many as 20 countries have monuments or statues to him.

summary: Ho Chi Minh (1890–1969) was a Vietnamese communist revolutionary who spent three decades abroad, founded the Indochinese Communist Party and led the Việt Minh to victory over France. As president of North Vietnam he ruled a one-party state, carried out a land reform with many executions and directed the war for the South until his death.

notes: Birth: the article gives 19 May 1890 as generally accepted, but says he used four other birth years (1891, 1892, 1894, 1895) and that early details are disputed; circa is set false, as the article gives the date; the editor may prefer true.
Names: the text uses the article's Vietnamese spellings (Hồ Chí Minh, Việt Minh, Điện Biên Phủ); the profile name is 'Ho Chi Minh' as given. Gold-link patterns may need the diacritic forms.
His stays in the United States and Britain (1912-1919) rest on his own claims and thin evidence (one letter, a postcard, a plaque); kept vague. The Brazil episode is left out.
Hồ Chí Minh trail: built from 1959 by 30,000 men, per the article.

Land reform figures: given as the article attributes them (Porter 1973, Szalontai 2007; the 'nearly 100,000' extrapolation and the 50,000 estimate 'widely accepted by scholars at the time'); Vo Nhan Tri's 15,000 wrongful executions left out for space.
The Phan Bội Châu betrayal: the article dates the arrest to June 1925.
The 'French shit' quotation is left out, as the article says its authenticity is challenged (Liam Kelley).

Left out for space: Zeng Xueming and Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai, the OSS medical treatment, the Ben-Gurion meeting, the Maneli, Seaborn, Ronning and Marigold peace channels, the Chinese support troops, the languages he spoke.
